Osteoarthritis Systemic corticosteroids are not considered to have a place in the management of osteoarthritis (p.11); however, intra- articular injection may be useful for acute exacerbations of joint pain and inflammation. Such injections should be given only infrequently and as adjunctive therapy. Osteopetrosis Osteopetrosis is a rare set of heterogeneous disorders char- acterised by an increase in bone density, generally due to a failure of the osteoclasts to resorb mineralised bone. In the severe infantile malignant form there is reduction in the bone marrow space, leading to anaemia, hepatosplenome- galy, and nerve compression that may produce blindness and deafness; early death often results. The adult form is benign; patients typically present with fractures, back and bone pain, but no haematological abnormalities, and gen- erally have a full life expectancy.1 Bone marrow transplantation may be curative for the in- fantile malignant form if a suitable donor can be found.1,2 Corticosteroids are used palliatively. Benefit has been re- ported in 3 of 4 children treated with oral prednisone 1 mg/kg daily, with phosphate supplements and a low-cal- cium diet.3 Some patients have also benefited from the use of high-dose calcitriol, again with a low-calcium diet.
